newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Annan spells out agenda debate on Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Annan spells out agenda debate on Zaire talks.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said that if a ceasefire could be brokered in Zaire between government forces and rebels then the Security Council might send troops to bolster the peace.
Annan, visiting Africa for the first time as head of the United Nations, told a news conference he was optimistic that a summit scheduled in Lome, Togo, on March 26 would lead Zaire towards peace.

He said both the rebels and the Zairean government had accepted a five-point U.N. peace plan in principle, but said the two sides remained at loggerheads over whether a ceasefire should precede or follow direct talks.
President Mobutu Sese Seko's government wanted to follow the U.N. timetable that first sets a ceasefire followed by talks and access for humanitarian organisations to refugees.

Laurent Kabila's rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, which has taken control of a fifth of Zaire and threatens to take the capital, Kinshasa, wants to reverse the order.
The rebels were not invited to a summit of African leaders in Nairobi on Wednesday.

"The Kabila group would prefer to see talks precede a ceasefire," Annan said. "But from what I have picked up about the discussions in Nairobi, attempts will be made to move ahead simultaneously on a ceasefire, talks and the design of a mechanism to mnitor the ceasefire."

Kabila told reporters after talks with South African President Nelson Mandela earlier on Thursday that the Security Council would consider deploying troops to monitor a ceasefire if there was evidence it would hold.
Annan said he would expect Africa to play a significant role in any monitoring force for Zaire and hoped South Africa would make a contribution.

"We would welcome the participation of as many African countries as possible. There has to be an African component. The days when African troops were kept back and troops from outside Africa came in are gone," he said.

South Africa has not sent troops outside its borders since the transition from white rule to democracy in 1994, but Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said the government was willing in principle to contribute to a peace-keeping operation.
Mandela, who launched an inconclusive personal initiative earlier this month to bring the two sides together in Cape Town, said he thought Kabila was committed to a negotiated settlement.

"In almost all the discussions we have had with him, he is insisting on meeting President Mobutu. Despite the successes he has achieved in the battlefield, he realises the importance of negotiations," he said.
Mandela said he and Annan also discussed the delayed installation of a government of national unity in Angola, the Sudan, the Middle East tension and plans to restructure the United Nations.
